newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Markets give cool welcome to British budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Markets give cool welcome to British budget.

text.p: British financial markets gave a cool reception to finance minister Kenneth Clarke's 1997/98 budget on Tuesday, unconvinced it would achieve his aim of reducing the risk of higher interest rates.
Shares ended higher but off pre-budget highs, government bonds finished lower, while sterling was sturdy.

The speech delivered the expected one percentage point cut in the basic rate of income tax, but Clarke surprised markets with a large cut in forecast government borrowing in fiscal 1997/98 that starts next April.

"It is politically astute and in the main, financially sound, but the budget is unlikely to deter speculation that another rate hike is just a matter of time," Rob Hayward, economist at BankAmerica in London, said.
"The good news is that the budget provides for fiscal tightening, the bad news is that it does not do enough."
Overall tax cuts amounted to 2.0 billion pounds ($3.34 billion), below market expectations of around 2.25 billion.

"This budget tightens fiscal policy," Clarke told the House of Commons, the lower house of parliament. "I am tightening fiscal policy now to reduce the risk of having to tighten monetary policy excessively as I set policy to hit my inflation target."

The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares closed up 13.8 points, or 0.34 percent, at 4,068.4 but well down from its the record high of 4,094.4 struck in early trading following Wall Street's record-breaking performance on Monday.
December FTSE futures were quoted at 4,095.0, up 29.0 points but off their 4,108.0 level before Clarke stood up to deliver his budget speech. the speech.

The 10-year benchmark government bond, or gilt, was quoted at 100.44 for a yield of 4.433 percent, rock steady on pre-budget levels. In the futures market, December gilts closed pit trading at 110-28, off 8/32 on the day and versus 111-07 before the speech.

The pound was quoted at 2.5523 marks compared with a fresh 32-month high of 2.5586 hit before the speech and up from 2.5409 late on Monday. Against the dollar, the pound was trading at $1.6745 compared with $1.6692 pre-budget.

The best part of the speech for markets was a cut in projected government spending next year of 19.0 billion pounds, below market forecasts of around 21 billion and well off the Treasury's summer forecast of 23.1 billion.

But markets were less pleased with a hike in growth forecasts to 3.5 percent in 1997 from summer predictions of 3.25 percent, prompting speculation that inflation in the already bubbling British economy could begin to accelerate.
Clarke forecast consumer spending would grow by three percent in 1996 and more than four percent in 1997. Analysts were unconvinced Clarke could keep to his 2.5 percent inflation target.

"It's a package which will give a considerable stimulus to consumer spending. It is dressed up very respectably in that there is quite a signficant downward revision to the PSBR. But I think in the end that that downward revision has much to do with growth as it is to do with anything else," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse.
Other highlights included a three pence increase in a litre of petrol and diesel fuel and an increase in the threshold for inheritance tax to 215,000 pounds from 200,000.

Corporation tax on small companies was cut to 23 percent, affecting 400,000 British firms but the main rate of corporation tax was left unchanged at 33 percent. Duties on beer and wine were left unchanged.
